name: Wendy Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the filler and the labeller on line two at a soft-drinks bottling plant just outside town. Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, and my job is keeping the bottles moving: topping up the caps hopper, clearing jams, swapping label reels and pulling samples for the lab every hour. When something stops, everyone looks at me first, because a stopped line costs money by the minute. I've been there six years now, since I finished my certificate.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can hear when something's wrong before the screen tells me. There's a rattle the capper makes before it jams, and I love catching it. What wears me out is the twelve hours on concrete and the pay, which is lower than the brewery in the city, but the brewery's an hour away and I don't drive. I rent a room in a shared house on Mill Street, and I've got about two weeks' rent saved if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, the robots aren't coming after all. At work we'd joke that the planning software still can't work out a holiday rota. Online I'd share something about how we should be talking about fair pay instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a bit of a relief, but my life's still tight. I'm still on low pay, still one bad month from asking my mum for money. The plant's fine for now, but nothing about AI going quiet fixes the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep pushing at the union branch for the pay review we were promised. I might use the chat tool on my phone now and then to help write a letter about the shift allowance, because it's good at that. I'd try to save something, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, but tired. Nothing's on fire, but nothing's getting better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two weeks of rent saved. What would you do if you lost a few shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for overtime on line one, and if that didn't come I'd go to my mum's for Sunday dinners to save on food. Losing two shifts at the bottling plant means I'm eating at my mum's on Sundays and walking instead of taking the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the plant itself that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer peak hides how quiet winter is. Last winter they cut us to three shifts a week for six weeks, and I nearly didn't make rent. If that happens again, I'm in trouble, AI or no AI.

say: I'd joke at work that the **planning software** still can't sort a rota.
I'd post that we should talk about **fair pay**, not robots.
think: I think it's a relief, but I'm still **one bad month** from asking my mum for money.
I think the **winter shift cuts** are the real danger, not AI.
do: Push the **union branch** for the pay review we were promised.
Use the **chat tool** sometimes to help write letters about the shift allowance.
Save at least **fifty a month** from my wages.
feel: **Calm-ish** but tired, because nothing is getting better either.
S0.quote: Losing two shifts at the bottling plant means I'm eating at my mum's on Sundays and walking instead of taking the bus.
fieldNote: Wendy's pressures are **seasonal shift cuts** and a tiny cushion, both unrelated to AI.
She uses AI **now and then** for practical things like letters, without fuss.
She is proud of her **ear for machines**, which gives her some confidence.

steps.text: Push the union branch for the promised pay review
Save fifty a month from bottling plant wages
Use the phone chat tool to draft the shift allowance letter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that's going to feel it first, the planners and the lab paperwork. At work I'd tell people to get on the union training list before it fills up. Online I'd share stuff about making companies pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our line gets a robot palletiser and a camera that checks the labels, and then they need fewer of us per shift. I'd probably keep my job for a while because I can fix things, but four operators on a line might become two. I'm not the best on the line, I'm in the middle, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my supervisor about the maintenance apprenticeship they run every couple of years, because the fitters will be needed longer than us. I'd start using the AI tool on my phone to learn about pneumatics, a bit each night. I'd join the union's working group on new machines, so we get a say in how they come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but like I can do something about it. It's the kind of worry that makes you get up and do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your day would change first in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hourly sample paperwork would go to a camera and software, and the stock ordering too. Then a robot would stack the pallets at the end, which is Paul's job now. My colleague Paul has stacked pallets at the bottling plant for twenty years, and a robot would do his job by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at maintenance. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money and time, mostly. The apprenticeship pays less than I earn now for the first year, and I can't drop to that on my rent. If the union got them to keep our pay during the course, I'd sign tomorrow.

say: I'd say the **office** feels it first, the planners and lab paperwork.
I'd tell colleagues to get on the **union training list** before it fills.
think: I think a **robot palletiser** and label cameras mean fewer operators per shift.
I think four operators could become **two**, and I'm only middling.
do: Ask my supervisor about the **maintenance apprenticeship** the plant runs.
Learn about **pneumatics** each night with the AI tool on my phone.
Join the union's **working group** on new machines.
feel: **Nervous**, but the kind of worry that makes me act.
S1.quote: My colleague Paul has stacked pallets at the bottling plant for twenty years, and a robot would do his job by spring.
fieldNote: Wendy reads the risk clearly: **fewer operators** per shift, not a closed plant.
Her barrier to retraining is the **apprenticeship pay cut**, not willingness.
She wants workers to have **a say** in how machines come in.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor about the plant's maintenance apprenticeship
Study pneumatics each night using the AI tool on her phone
Join the union working group on new machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from the government, right now, because companies won't look after us. At work I'd be telling everyone to stick together. Online I'd probably be one of those people posting about a robot tax every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the bottling line is one of the easiest things in the world to automate. In 2028 the planning and ordering go overnight, and by 2031 a robot can clear jams and swap reels. I'd be 32 with a certificate for a job that doesn't exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course straight away, even at the lower pay, because three years is all I've got. I'd move back in with my mum to make that possible. I'd get the union to push for a hiring freeze until we've all been retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. A proper cold feeling, not the nervous kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028, and robots for hands-on work around 2031. What does that three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is enough to get a maintenance ticket if I start the week it's announced. After that, the people fixing the robots might last a bit longer than the people running the line. Three years of warning is just enough to get a maintenance ticket, if I start the week the news breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd ask your mum for money. Would you move back home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, and I'd hate it. My mum's flat has one bedroom, so it'd be the sofa. I'd do it for a year if it got me a trade.

say: I'd say the **government** needs a plan now, because companies won't protect us.
I'd post about a **robot tax** online every day.
think: I think a bottling line is one of the **easiest** things to automate.
I think I'd be **32** with a certificate for a job that's gone.
do: Start the **maintenance course** straight away, even at lower pay.
Move back in with my **mum** to afford the course.
Get the union to push for a **hiring freeze** until we're retrained.
feel: **Scared**, a cold feeling, not the nervous kind.
S2.quote: Three years of warning is just enough to get a maintenance ticket, if I start the week the news breaks.
fieldNote: Wendy uses the **three-year gap** concretely: just enough for a maintenance ticket.
She'd accept a **sofa at her mum's** to make retraining possible.
She still expects to **lose her operator job** and says so without softening it.

steps.text: Start the maintenance course at the bottling plant on lower pay
Move onto the sofa at her mum's flat for a year
Push the union for a hiring freeze until operators are retrained

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them properly and not panic. At work I'd keep pushing the union to get retraining paid for. Online I'd share what's actually working in other countries, if I could find it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the operator job, just later. But eight years before the robots is enough time to become the person who fixes them, if I'm smart about it. It still worries me, because fitters might not be safe forever either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see which machines our plant actually buys, then train on those. I'd save properly first, aiming for two months' rent, so I don't need the sofa. I'd use the AI tools more at home to learn the electrical side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. It feels like a problem I can work through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, robots around 2034. Would you do things in a different order than in the fast picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd save first and train second, so I don't end up broke. Five years means I can save two months' rent first, then train on whatever robots the bottling plant actually buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea from maintenance, because she knows what's coming before management tells us. Then my mum, because she worries.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so we should use them properly.
I'd push the union to get **retraining paid for**.
think: I think I'd still **lose the operator job**, just later.
I think eight years is enough to become the person who **fixes the robots**.
do: Wait a year to see which **machines** the plant buys.
Save **two months' rent** before starting any course.
Use AI tools at home to learn the **electrical side**.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like a problem I can work through.
S3.quote: Five years means I can save two months' rent first, then train on whatever robots the bottling plant actually buys.
fieldNote: The extra years let Wendy **sequence** her plan: save first, then train.
She trusts **Bea from maintenance** more than management for early warning.
She remains **anxious** because she expects to lose her current role.

steps.text: Save two months of rent before starting a course
Watch which robots the bottling plant buys for a year
Learn the electrical side at home using AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no reason for anyone to be thrown on the scrap heap with ten years' warning. At work I'd say let's plan this together, union and company. Online I'd be less loud, more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine if I use the time. Ten years is enough to do the apprenticeship slowly, save up and get a maintenance job somewhere. I still wouldn't feel safe, because my pay is low and nothing's guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance apprenticeship in two or three years, when my rent's sorted. I'd keep going to union meetings so the company pays for it. I'd use AI on my phone more, like everyone else, once the plant starts using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a knot underneath. Like a plan I believe in, but not completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years for AGI, robots around 2039. What would you be doing at 35, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 35 I'd like to be the fitter Bea is now, with a van and a toolbox, not standing at the filler. My plan at 35 is a fitter's van and a toolbox, not twelve hours standing at a filler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow picture that still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The winters, still. In every picture, if they cut shifts for six weeks, I'm short on rent. That doesn't change with ten years.

say: I'd say nobody should be **thrown away** with ten years' warning.
I'd say the **union and company** should plan this together.
think: I think I'd be **fine** if I use the time well.
I think **low pay** still means nothing is guaranteed.
do: Start the **maintenance apprenticeship** in two or three years.
Keep going to **union meetings** so the company pays for training.
Use **AI on my phone** more once the plant uses it.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a knot underneath about winter shift cuts.
S4.quote: My plan at 35 is a fitter's van and a toolbox, not twelve hours standing at a filler.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Wendy's mood stays **anxious** because winter shift cuts threaten rent.
Her goal at 35 is a **fitter's van**, a concrete picture of the future.
She trusts the plan but not **completely**, which she says herself.

steps.text: Start the plant maintenance apprenticeship in two or three years
Keep attending union meetings to get training paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years is barely enough to retrain and I'd be on my mum's sofa doing it. What would help is paid retraining, where you keep your wage while you learn, and a union that has a real say in how the robots come in. I don't need a robot tax speech, I need my rent paid while I learn to fix the robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about winter. Every scenario sounded like it was about AI, but for people like me the worst months are when the drinks don't sell. I'd want help with that too.

headlineQuote: I don't need a robot tax speech, I need my rent paid while I learn to fix the robot.
portrait: Wendy, 27, runs the **filler and labeller** at a bottling plant and rents a room with two weeks' rent saved.
She is **union-minded**, practical, and proud of hearing machine faults before the screen shows them.
She uses AI **now and then** and would retrain into maintenance if her pay were protected.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, and stays anxious otherwise.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years barely covers retraining and she'd be on her mum's sofa.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** that keeps her wage, plus a union say in how robots arrive.
